hook.text: J.I. Rodale brought organic farming to America in 1942. Doctors and scientists called him a crank.

buildup.text: Rodale published Organic Farming and Gardening magazine, preaching composting and chemical-free growing.

discovery.text: His Farming Systems Trial—started in 1981—is the longest-running comparison of organic and conventional farming.

twist.text: After 40 years, the trial shows organic yields match conventional after a transition period—with lower input costs.

climax.text: Rodale's once-fringe ideas are now mainstream. Organic food is a $200 billion global industry.

punchline.text: The crank was right. It just took 80 years for the world to listen.

quiz.question: What does the Rodale Farming Systems Trial show after 40 years?
options: Organic yields match conventional after transition, with lower input costs

details.summary: J.I. Rodale founded a publishing and farming empire in the 1940s that popularized organic agriculture in the United States. His Organic Farming and Gardening magazine and the Rodale Institute brought Howard's ideas to millions of American farmers and gardeners.
details.whyItMatters: Rodale transformed organic farming from an obscure philosophy into a mainstream American movement. The Rodale Institute's long-running trials provided scientific evidence that organic methods can match conventional yields.
takeaways: J.I. Rodale launched Organic Farming and Gardening magazine in 1942
The Rodale Institute conducts the longest-running organic vs. conventional trial
Rodale's advocacy helped build the consumer demand that drives organic markets today

faq.question: What is the Rodale Institute's Farming Systems Trial?
faq.answer: Started in 1981, this is the longest-running side-by-side comparison of organic and conventional farming in North America. It has shown that organic systems can match conventional yields after a transition period while improving soil health and using less energy.

faq.question: How did J.I. Rodale influence American agriculture?
faq.answer: Rodale published magazines and books that translated complex organic farming science into practical advice for everyday farmers and gardeners. He built a media and research empire that brought organic ideas into millions of American households.
